1:
Adam Clarke reads the chapter as a hymn diversified by changes of speaker, and lays out the parts: a chorus of the Church celebrating God’s protection and setting the happiness of the righteous against the misery of the wicked; their own resolution to obey and trust; then the prophet breaking in, catching up the last words of the chorus and repeating them as one musical instrument reverberates the sound of another tuned to the same key; then a chorus confessing sin, a gracious reply promising deliverance like life from the dead, and a closing exhortation to patience that alludes to the night of the destroying angel. Charles Ellicott has the prophet appear once more as a psalmist, writing for the worship of the new city itself. John Gill dates the singing to the destruction of the church’s enemies and notes that the old paraphrase calls it a new song; John Wesley that it is sung in the church of God.

John Calvin asks when it was written rather than when it will be sung. The prophet composed it before the calamity fell, so the people might be the better prepared to endure it—not merely to give thanks after their deliverance, but so that in captivity, when they were like dead men, they might strengthen their hearts with it, train their children in the expectation, and hand the promises down to posterity. He adds that the song was despised when published, the good men of that generation being very few; and that when the temple was down and the city sacked they might fairly have asked where these gates were that they were bidden to open, and who was to enter them.

On the city Matthew Henry supplies the charter: it is incorporated by the everlasting covenant and fitted to receive all that charter makes free, strong as the old city was while it stood compact, with God himself a wall of fire about it and salvation appointed for its defence. Ellicott presses the same point—those walls are not of stone or brick but are themselves a living force, saving and protecting—and would render the clause as salvation he appoints. Wesley reduces it to God’s immediate protection standing to the church instead of walls. Clarke turns to the words: the strong city is set against the enemy city just destroyed, and the second noun means properly the ditch outside the wall, so the pair are the wall and its outwork; on the same authority he reports that the song belongs to the days of the Messiah.

The opened gates draw the widest range of readings. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the city has so far been thought of as empty, being like paradise first of all a creation of God, so the cry is a heavenly one and those commanded to open, if we may ask at all, must be angels. Ellicott hears the same cry from the heralds of the city’s king, and takes the last word as a plural covering every form of truthfulness. Gill will have neither literal gatekeepers nor angelic ones, and applies the command to the ministers of the gospel who hold the key of knowledge. Clarke makes it the entrance of the converted Gentiles as fellow heirs, the middle wall of partition broken down, and takes the truth for the gospel itself against the shadowy rites it fulfils. Henry reads a repeal of the laws that had banished the righteous, or rather an act naturalizing them of whatever nation, and observes that states do well to countenance such men, since they bring a blessing with them. Calvin finds in the title the fruit of the chastisement: the Church was always a barn where chaff is mixed with wheat, but those who came back had undertaken a long and dangerous journey when many preferred to stay, so a purer body returned than had gone.
3:
The famous promise is shorter in the original than in the English. John Gill points out that the word perfect is not in the Hebrew at all, which simply says peace, peace, the doubling standing for the certainty and the continuance of it and covering every sort—peace with God and with men, inward and outward, here and hereafter. Adam Clarke renders it peace upon peace, all kinds of prosperity in this world and the next. Charles Ellicott says the italics of the English betray how much has been interpolated, and offers a barer version: thou establishest a purpose firm; peace, peace, for in thee is his trust—completeness being expressed by iteration, since no adjective could add to the fulness of the noun. Keil and Delitzsch take the sentence for a maxim, borrowed later by a psalm, and gloss the noun as the whole inward attitude and habit of a man as a creature of thought and will, which has a firm hold in itself only when it has a firm hold on God.

John Calvin turns the sentence the other way round. The word may mean imagination, creature, or thought, and others render it of the settled foundation or the fixed mind of the believer; but he would refer the firmness to God, so that the peace of the Church rests on his eternal and unchangeable purpose. His argument is grammatical and theological at once: if the steadfastness were the believer’s, the clause that follows, giving trust as the reason, would be superfluous. And he finds an implied contrast in it between God’s fixed thought and our wandering ones, since something new springs up almost every moment to drive our thoughts about, and no change however slight fails to breed a doubt; we do wrong, he says, to judge an unshaken purpose by such fickle imaginations. The repetition means uninterrupted continuance, and by peace he understands not serenity of mind only but every kind of happiness. Clarke, characteristically, records that the old versions differ on the last verb, one giving they have trusted and two we have trusted, while a grammarian defends the received reading as impersonal.

The exhortation that follows rests on a rare divine name, and the commentators divide over how much to make of it. Keil and Delitzsch call the doubled name the proper name of God the Redeemer in its most emphatic form, met with only here and in one earlier place, and say that in it there is an everlasting rock—he is essentially such a rock. Ellicott notes the same rarity and renders the last phrase literally as the Rock of Ages, the phrase of the well-known hymn, the name standing for the unchangeableness of God. Clarke goes further, reporting a rabbinical rendering that makes it the eternal Fountain or Spring, and asking whether the lasting streams from the rock in the desert are not in view—and that rock, he adds, was Christ. Calvin refuses both liberties. He rejects as forced the reading that turns the noun into an adjective and gives the strong God of ages, and he sees little ground for the ingenuity of those who draw the divinity of Christ from the doubled name, as though the prophet were saying that one name is in the other; the two names are given, in his view, for the express purpose of magnifying God’s power. That power is not power lying unemployed but power actively exerted, carrying to its end what it began; and since it is perpetual, faith must be perpetual too, rising above the world by continual advances. Gill and John Wesley keep to the plain sense of the adverb, that the trust is for all times and conditions, in affliction and temptation and darkness alike.
5:
The fall of the proud city has the poor for its instrument. Keil and Delitzsch say the rock has already proved itself one on which everything breaks that attacks those it surrounds, and note that the song passes beyond the fall of Moab to the imperial city itself, to which Moab was only an annex; the doubling in the line, elsewhere a link between variant forms, here changes only the form of a suffix. Charles Ellicott identifies the same great city of confusion, and finds the humiliation sharpened because the instruments of its destruction are the very people it had oppressed. John Wesley takes the height for dignity and power, not situation. John Calvin insists the two halves belong together, since it would be no full consolation to hear the proud laid low without hearing the lowly set in their room; he takes the city to include not only fortifications, which the ancients built in high places, but wealth and magnificence, and observes that towers do not displease God in themselves, only that the strong are so rarely not proud. Matthew Henry adds that God can do it however well fortified the place, has often done it, and makes it his glory; and that the text does not say great armies shall tread them down, but the feet of the poor. John Gill supplies the treading—mire in the streets, grapes in the winepress, grass under cattle—and denies that a prince’s foot is meant.

The even way divides the readings. Gill offers three: the way appointed for the just is uprightness itself; or evenness, so plain that fools shall not err in it; or the way of the Lord towards the just is evenness, with no inequality in it though it is often charged with some. Ellicott finds the English tautologous and would read is straight, leading without interruption to its appointed end, and for the obscure weighing of the path would put makest smooth; he suspects the vocative most upright is adverbial. Keil and Delitzsch make the smoothing a rolling, so the road lies as if bevelled with a rule, and note that the song has fallen into proverb and pauses here as at a strophe’s end. Calvin denies that the verse praises the righteousness of the godly at all: the metaphor is of God applying a balance and bringing to an equal measure things in themselves unequal, so the rough ways are made plain however they look. Without that, he says, no one would make way among so many thorns and briers, steep roads, windings and rough places. Wesley keeps the weighing and makes it examination followed by approval; Henry takes both—an even steady course the just keep, and a path God levels by removing what would trip them.

The waiting comes last, and Calvin makes it the test. By the judgments he understands adversity, and here is the mark that divides the godly from hypocrites: in prosperity the hypocrite blesses God and speaks highly of him, but in adversity murmurs and curses, judging of God by how long the prosperity lasts, while the godly are the more stirred to confidence the harder they are tried. Gill allows two senses for the judgments—the ordinances, attendance on which is the right way of waiting, or the chastisements measured out in mercy—and concludes they had followed God not only in the even way but the rugged one. Keil and Delitzsch have the church of the last days looking back and telling with what longing it had waited for the manifestation now granted, against those who think the prophet has dropped from the ideal to his actual present. Ellicott takes the name for what reveals God’s character and will, so those who waited in the path of his judgments ask a fuller showing of it. Adam Clarke notes that three of the old versions read the verb without its pronoun.
9:
The night watch is read three ways. John Gill allows it literally, or of the captivity, which one old expositor called a night, or of the darkness before Christ came. Charles Ellicott makes it the time of sorrow and expectation in which the saints watch for the morning, and notes that soul and spirit are joined to express the fulness of personality. John Calvin distinguishes the two words as the will and the understanding, the chief parts of the soul, and rejects the reading that makes one the regenerate part and the other the natural soul, since the merely natural man never seeks God at all. His gloss on the night is that no hour is too unseasonable for prayer: the time set apart for rest, when a sleeper and a dead man differ little, is when he rises to seek God—not that sleepers think, but that sleep itself, if we are turned towards God, belongs to our course, and we praise him by hope while silent. John Wesley puts it plainly: his thoughts work towards God while others sleep. Adam Clarke would put the last clause in the past—when thy judgments were in the earth, the inhabitants have learned righteousness—and adds that men seldom seek God in prosperity, resting in an earthly portion till he embitters it in mercy.

The next verse looks like a contradiction, and Calvin says so. He has just had the world learning righteousness from judgments; now the wicked cannot be won by kindness either. His answer is that the profit was never universal—scourges made Pharaoh only more obstinate—and that the earlier statement meant the elect, with whom some hypocrites share a portion, moved however reluctantly by reverence or dread of punishment. He rejects the reading that makes the clause a question and keeps it a concession: whatever kindness God draws them with, they will never learn to act uprightly. He refuses too to limit the land of uprightness to one country, since wherever men now call on God’s name that title holds, and the ingratitude is the worse for it. Keil and Delitzsch agree it is a hypothetical clause with the condition left to the emphasis, and gloss the land as one where everything is right and all goes honourably—where a worthless man would still act wickedly. Ellicott says as much in a poet’s line, that the mind is its own place and can make a hell of heaven itself; the eyes that see the majesty of the Lord are those of the pure in heart. Gill lists the favours—the good things of this life, exemption from common troubles, sometimes the means of grace—and Wesley sets the wicked man’s course against the believer’s in every condition.

On the lifted hand the readings turn on tense. Ellicott would have they did not see, to sharpen the contrast with what follows: when the arm was raised only to protect God’s people the evildoers shut their eyes, and judgment alone will make them look. He would also read the next clause as their seeing, to their shame, God’s jealousy for his people. Calvin says the majesty meant is not the hidden one but what is visible in God’s works, which the hand stands for by a figure; ignorance cannot be pleaded, since the hand is lifted up and not merely exerted. The later seeing differs from the first: they shall see too late, like men before them who fled God’s face and were still made to know their Judge. The envy is what the wicked feel on comparing their lot with the godly’s; the fire is a metaphor for the severest vengeance, though Calvin allows an allusion to the cities burned in the old story. Gill has them refusing to trace visible punishment to God, laying it to chance or second causes; Wesley has them learning by sad experience what they would not learn by easier ways.
12:
The confession that God has wrought all our works divides the two most theological readers. Matthew Henry takes it at full strength: whatever good work is done by us is owing to a good work wrought by grace in us, God putting the good thought and affection into the heart, so that being acted upon we act; and whatever kindness is shown us he works for us, sometimes making that work for us which seemed to work against us. John Calvin pulls back. He grants that God alone does what is good in us, but says that those who quote this verse to overturn free will have not understood the prophet, who is only showing that all the good we enjoy came from God’s hand; and he adds that it is not worth pressing in that controversy, since an opponent might easily evade it and there are many passages far more conclusive. On the promise itself he glosses ordain as establish—peace prepared in uninterrupted succession, where the peace of the wicked is short—and Charles Ellicott would render the second clause for us rather than in us, the work being the great work of salvation. John Gill takes the peace as outward and inward at once, and chiefly of the latter day.

The other lords are variously identified. Gill runs through the possibilities—sin and Satan in the unregenerate, the idols called lords, which he rejects because that word is not used here, the native governors of the old paraphrase, the Assyrians and Babylonians—and settles on persecuting tyrants. Ellicott takes them for the conquerors, and possibly for the false gods they identified themselves with; he would read the second clause as through thee alone we celebrate thy name, the power to praise having been restored by God’s hand and not man’s strength. John Wesley distinguishes foreign and heathen lords from the governors God had himself set up. Calvin makes that distinction the heart of the verse: not every prince rules besides God, since a good king rules in his name, but only those opposed to true worship—and the complaint fits any people compelled by unjust laws to observe a superstition. Henry hears a confession of sin in it as much as a complaint, and turns it penitentially: every lust has been our lord.

On the dead who shall not rise, Keil and Delitzsch warn against the obvious inference. The verse does not deny a resurrection—the prophet knew of one, as the chapter will show—but speaks of the oppressors, thrust down among the shades with no possibility of rising again. Calvin argues the same from the structure, since the nineteenth verse states the opposite and the contrast between the two resurrections would be lost otherwise; and he insists on shades rather than the alternative rendering for the same reason. Ellicott improves the line by dropping the supplied words—dead, they live not; shadows, they rise not—puts them in the gloomy world from which there was for them no escape, and records the odd Greek version making it physicians who shall not raise them. Wesley says only that the tyrants shall never rise to molest us again. The closing increase is contested too. Gill and Keil and Delitzsch take the growing nation for the church or for Israel numerous once more, the latter hearing behind these verses the bondage in Egypt, the drowning of Pharaoh, and the borders of the land under David and Solomon. Ellicott reports a Greek rendering that turns the clause into a prayer for evils on the glorious, and prefers thou hast moved far off the borders of the land, meaning an ideal restoration to the old remoter boundaries; Wesley, on the contrary, reads a removal into captivity. Calvin sees the calling of the Gentiles: a kingdom once confined within narrow limits extended, not by enlarging the land but by spreading the worship of God till intercourse gave larger room.
16:
The verse about visiting God in trouble is doubtful in almost every word. Charles Ellicott would render it have they missed thee, or sought after, or remembered thee, and notes that the noun for prayer is a peculiar one, used elsewhere of the whispered incantations of the heathen and meaning here the low-toned prayers of the afflicted, pitched as in a minor key. Adam Clarke reports the Greek and two manuscripts putting the verb in the first person plural—in affliction we have sought thee—thinks the next word may be first person too, and calls the last clause extremely obscure, the Greek reading on us for on them, a frequent sort of mistake. Keil and Delitzsch take the whole as the prayer looking back on the night of affliction that preceded the redemption. John Calvin weighs whether it describes hypocrites, who flee to God only under constraint, and decides for believers, since God instructs them by chastisement too; the bitterness is sweetened by the result, and the godly are nearer God in affliction than in the prosperity that makes us proud. On the strange noun he agrees with Ellicott without the philology: it is not a prayer pronounced in words but what a heart wrung with pain produces, since men speak with open mouths in prosperity and can hardly venture to mutter when cast down—the unutterable groans of the apostle. John Gill and John Wesley keep the plain sense, that the afflicted frequent the throne of grace, and that this is sometimes the very end the affliction serves.

The figure of the woman in labour is handled most closely by Calvin, who marks two things in it. The first is the intensity: the anguish is not merely that of outward distress but the dreadful pain of the godly heart when it perceives God angry and conscience reproves, which no bodily pain equals. The second is that the prophet breaks the metaphor. A woman forgets her sorrow at the sight of what she has brought forth, but the godly are continually bringing forth, and when they think the birth at hand they have nothing but fresh anguish; new troubles always await them, so we must never suppose our afflictions spent. Ellicott finds the image the natural one for longing expectation followed by joy, and reads the disappointment as a false pregnancy, a disease with no birth for its outcome—the as it were, he says, betrays the prophet’s awareness of how bold the figure is. Gill and Wesley put it simply, that they had the torment of childbearing without the comfort of a living child.

Clarke supplies a physician’s footnote to the same image. A learned professor, he reports, identified a specific disorder, a windy inflation of the womb, in which women have seemed to themselves and to skilful medical men to be pregnant, and after all the throes of apparent childbearing have been relieved by an emission of wind; the complaint, he says, is well known to the profession, and one old version seems to have read the line that way. He would also read in the land rather than in the earth. On the last clause the readings part. Calvin knows an interpretation that takes the verb as dwelling, which would mean that the exiles shall not return and the present possessors shall not perish, but prefers the ordinary sense and refers it to the wicked—the inhabitants of the world trouble us and do not fall, everything going prosperously with them—and recalls the old proverb that it is happiest not to be born, or being born to depart at once. Ellicott instead keeps the birth image to the end, since the verb for falling is used of a woman’s delivery, and renders it that the inhabitants of the world were not brought to birth; he notes too the Greek version making it those in the tombs who shall rise.
19:
The great promise of the chapter is the one place where the commentators must decide how much they will allow it. John Calvin canvasses the options and refuses all the narrow ones: many read it of the last resurrection only, the Jewish expositors of the days of the Messiah, whom he thinks mistaken in supposing it discharged at the first coming, and Christians equally mistaken in confining it to the last judgment—since the prophet takes in the whole reign of Christ from beginning to end. He is careful about who is promised life. It is not promised indiscriminately but to God’s dead men, believers who die in the Lord; the reprobate are dead while they live, having no taste of the fatherly kindness in which life consists, while believers obtain life in the midst of affliction and in death itself, though they are not said literally to live until the day when all is restored. On the noun he presses the worst word—putrefaction—and says the long decay by which they seem consumed will not hinder God from raising them entire.

The phrase about the prophet’s own body is grammatically loose, and each of them handles it differently. Calvin lists the renderings offered—with my dead body, who are my dead body, like as my dead body—and prefers to take the words in immediate connection, holding that the prophet inserts himself deliberately so as to join the whole Church and count himself among God’s dead men in the hope of the resurrection. John Wesley reads it exactly so: as I myself, who am one of these dead men, shall live again, you shall be delivered along with me; and he marks the contrast with the tyrants of the fourteenth verse, whose dead shall not live, where thine shall. Adam Clarke keeps to the manuscripts, reporting that all the ancient versions have the plural and that two of them give their dead bodies, a reading no manuscript yet found confirms. Charles Ellicott renders simply thy dead shall live, my corpses shall rise.

How far the verse teaches a bodily resurrection is the real question. Ellicott holds that the words, while implying a belief more or less distinct in one, are used primarily of a national and spiritual rising, like the vision of the dry bones and the apostle’s life from the dead. Clarke agrees that the deliverance is here explained by images plainly taken from the resurrection, and then turns the point round into an argument: an image assumed to represent something in allegory must be one commonly known and understood, or it will not answer the purpose it was assumed for—so the doctrine must already have been popular when the prophet wrote. He notes that Kimchi referred the words to the days of the Messiah, and adds his own question, whether they do not speak of the rising of Christ and of the bodies of men as its consequence, which he thinks very express. John Gill takes them for a promise of things that would be as life from the dead—conversions among Jews and Gentiles, a revival of religion grown cold, the slain witnesses living again—and then of the first resurrection at the second coming. On the dew the versions divide. Clarke would read the dew of the dawn on the authority of three old versions; Ellicott allows the dew of herbs, which quickens a withered plant as grace revives a dying people, but reports that most render it the dew of lights, born of the womb of the morning, and notes that the verb for casting out the dead is another form of the one used just before of childbirth. Wesley leaves it at the favour and blessing of God, which makes his people grow.
20:
Several of them think the chapter has already ended. Matthew Henry reports the view that these two verses begin a new matter and serve as an introduction to what follows rather than a conclusion to the song, and John Gill allows both, either a part of the song warning of trouble before the glory, or the opening of a fresh subject. Keil and Delitzsch say plainly that the song is at an end and the prophecy speaks once more as prophecy, and add that the standpoint of these chapters is incessantly oscillating backwards and forwards, so that the judgment is described after the completion of the church though it must actually have come first. Adam Clarke hears an allusion to the command given before the destroying angel went through the land, that none should go out at the door until morning, and to the order to stand still and see the salvation before the sea was crossed.

The chambers are given three characters by Henry: chambers of distinction, since those God has set apart ought to set themselves apart; chambers of defence, where a man hides himself as Noah did in the ark with the door shut behind him, or the prophet by the brook, on the principle that those are safest who are least seen; and chambers of devotion, the closet where one is private with God. He notes that the people had to keep within doors on the night of the firstborn, or the blood on the door-posts would not have secured them. John Calvin makes the chamber an inward one, calmness and composure of mind, like the watch-tower another prophet climbed to await the result in silence; and he presses the shutting of the door as steadfastness, since the devil will break in at the smallest chink left open. Charles Ellicott keeps both senses at once—men seek the innermost recesses of the house while the thunderstorm sweeps the city, and so are to seek God in solitary prayer—and John Wesley reduces it to withdrawing from the world and praying in the closet.

On the little moment Henry is at his most vivid: it is the smallest part of time we can conceive, an atom of matter, and with an as it were besides, so that it is less than we think; and he recalls a bishop banished from his city who told his grieving friends it was only a small cloud that would soon blow over. Calvin admits the difficulty honestly—afflictions continue as long as we live, so that in our own judgment they are of very long duration—and answers by the comparison with eternity. He takes the indignation for the affliction proceeding from God’s anger rather than the rage of enemies, though he does not object to the other reading. On the last verse Gill explains that God, being everywhere, cannot properly leave one place, but is said to come out of it as a king leaves his throne to go against an enemy; Calvin, whom Gill cites, prefers a reference to the sanctuary over one to heaven, since heathen nations despised the ark as laid up in a place little renowned and would learn that God comes forth from it at his own time. Ellicott reads a plural of intensity in the bloods, and has the earth bring to light first the blood of the slain and then the forms of the murdered themselves, as the ground once cried out for the first murder. Clarke turns it into an exclamation—what a reckoning the kingdoms of the earth will have for the torrents of blood shed to gratify the lust of power—and Wesley says only that the innocent blood shall be brought to light and severely revenged. Calvin closes it: the earth drinks the blood and seems to bury the memory, but the earth itself will take up arms to avenge it.
